text.en: Krishnan in Chennai tells Amir in Kashmir that it is cold today at 20 degrees Celsius. Amir laughs, for to him that feels warm. What is cold to one is pleasant to another. To talk about weather fairly we need common ways of measuring it. In this chapter we learn the elements of weather and the instruments that measure them.

Weather is the state of the atmosphere at a place at a given time: how hot or cold, wet or dry, windy or calm it is. It can change in a day. The atmosphere is the layer of air around the Earth. It has layers like a cake, and weather happens in the lowest layer, the troposphere, which extends 6 to 18 kilometres above the ground; it is thinner at the poles where cold air contracts and thicker in the tropics where warm air expands.
The elements of weather are temperature, precipitation, atmospheric pressure, wind and humidity. Temperature is how hot or cold the air is. Precipitation is any form of water that falls from the sky, such as rain, snow, sleet or hail. Sleet is frozen or partly frozen rain. Weather is different from climate, which is the average weather over many years.
Temperature is measured with a thermometer, in degrees Celsius or Fahrenheit. A thermometer uses a coloured liquid that expands when the temperature rises. 15 degrees Celsius equals 59 degrees Fahrenheit. Rainfall is measured with a rain gauge: a cylinder with a scale that shows the depth of collected water. If 5 mm of water collects we say 5 mm of rainfall. The gauge must stand on a flat place so it will not tilt or topple in the wind.
Atmospheric pressure is the weight of the air above us. It is measured by a barometer. At the sea coast it is about 1013 millibars; it falls as we climb a mountain. Climbers get less oxygen and must acclimatise. A fall in pressure below about 1000 millibars indicates a depression or low-pressure system, which can grow into a storm or a cyclone. Wind is the movement of air from high pressure to low pressure. Its direction is shown by a wind vane or wind sock and its speed is measured by an anemometer. Wind carries seeds and matters to pilots and sailors.
Humidity is the amount of water vapour present in the air. Relative humidity of 20 to 40 percent is dry weather, and 60 to 80 percent is humid weather. It is measured by a hygrometer. Museums monitor humidity to preserve their exhibits.
Readings are taken at regular intervals at weather stations and used to map and forecast weather. The India Meteorological Department (IMD) gathers the data, and in 2023 an automatic weather station was set up at a glacial lake in Sikkim at over 4,800 metres. Forecasts warn fishermen not to go to sea in storms and help to evacuate coasts before cyclones. In many parts of India people also read natural clues, such as pine cones that open and close with humidity, to guess the arrival of monsoon.

problem.en: The news says a town received 30 mm of rain in a day. What does it mean?

text.en: Rainfall is the depth of water collected in a rain gauge.
30 mm means the water would be 30 mm deep if it did not drain or evaporate.
A place with 30 mm in a day had considerable rain.

problem.en: Convert 25 degrees Celsius to Fahrenheit using F = C x 9/5 + 32.

text.en: Multiply 25 by 9/5 = 45.
So 25 degrees Celsius = 77 degrees Fahrenheit.

prompt.en: Name the five elements of weather and one instrument for each.

requiredIdeas.en: Pressure, barometer; wind, anemometer; humidity, hygrometer.

commonMisconceptions.en: Thinking wind blows from low to high pressure.

points.en: Weather is the state of the atmosphere at a time and place.
Its elements are temperature, precipitation, pressure, wind and humidity.
Each has an instrument: thermometer, rain gauge, barometer, anemometer, hygrometer.
